newsitem.title: USA: US hog tally near year ago Mar 1, seen increasing.
newsitem.headline: US hog tally near year ago Mar 1, seen increasing.

text.p: CHICAGO, March 25, Reuter - The number of hogs on U.S. farms as of March 1 was likely near year-ago levels but producers are moving into an expansion phase which should be reflected by Thursday's U.S. Agriculture Department Hogs and Pigs Report, livestock analysts said.
"The hog industry was in an expansion mode and the report will clearly indicate that, said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
However, dwindling small producers and environmental problems hampering big producers limited expansion, he said.
The USDA data will be released Thursday at 1400 CST/2000 GMT.

Analysts' estimates for all hogs and pigs on U.S. farms as of March 1 averaged 99.2 percent of a year ago and ranged from 97.0 to 100.9 percent. Estimates on hogs kept for breeding averaged 101.4 percent in a range of 98.5 to 104.0 percent and hogs kept for marketing averaged 99.0 percent of a year ago in a range of 96.0 to 100.8 pct.
Analysts said herd expansion, which probably already was under way, will likely be boosted by recent developments in Taiwan.

They referred to an indefinite ban Taiwan imposed on its pork exports last week linked to a foot and mouth disease outbreak in hogs there. Taiwan had been Japan's largest supplier of imported pork with the U.S. running second.
"What this ban on Taiwan exports will do is give producers who have been on the fence an even stronger signal to expand," said Karl Skold, director of research for Frontier Risk Management.
Producers struggled with high feed costs last year which pushed many small producers out of the market while larger operations struggled with enviromental issues.
But this did not stop expansion late in the year, analysts said.

"The things that are going to clearly indicate that expansion is going on, is the size of the breeding herd being above a year ago and larger farrowing intentions for the spring and summer of this year," Levitt said.

Analysts' estimates on March-May farrowing intentions averaged 102.9 percent of a year ago in a range of 102.0 to 105.0 percent and June-August intentions averaged 105.0 the previous year in a range of 103.0 to 107.0 percent.
Analysts were also looking for a revision to the December report, especially the breeding herd number, several said.

Skold said the December report implied fall gilt retention was down about 20 percent from the previous year but he said the number was likely near even with a year ago. This would account for the wide range of estimates on this report's breeding herd number as some analysts factored in a revision and others did not, he said.
But recent developments in Taiwan are expected to overshadow most any numbers on Thursday's report.

Exports were already expected to be larger in the last half of 1997 and "now there is a tremendous potential to have exports well above what anyone dreamed of," because of the Taiwan situation, Skold said.

Levitt noted that the industry being in an expansion mode would have been viewed as bearish, with slaughter in the last half of the year up four to five percent. But now those numbers would be tolorable becasuse of the Taiwan situation.

"The outlook for pork expanded significantly with Taiwan's pork exports ban...that gave new life to the pork market for this year," Levitt said. "The expansion that shows up in the Hog and Pig report will not be large enough to diminish that."

"We have a clear chance now to spend most of the year at or above the $50 per cwt level for live hogs or certainly above the $70 level for lean hogs even through the latter part of the year. And between now and summer a move by lean hogs to $85 or $90 is now clearly possible," Levitt added.
((Chicago Newsdesk 312-408-8725))
